note: Ten more chapters for the intelligence explosion page. Words are my own summaries. Numbers are copied from the linked sources, checked on 29 October 2026.

chapters.alt: A river of city lights runs flat for a long way and then shoots straight up into the night sky
chapters.h: Growth has been speeding up for ages
chapters.lead: Zoom out far enough and the whole human story looks like one long take off. That is why some economists take the idea of an explosion seriously, and why others push back.

points.v: In 2020 David Roodman of Open Philanthropy fitted a statistical model to gross world product from 10,000 BCE to 2019. Growth has tended to speed up as the economy grew, not stay constant.
If that pattern simply continued, his model sends output to infinity in finite time. The median year for that explosion came out as 2047, give or take 16 years.
Roodman says it would not really reach infinity. He reads it as a sign the human system is unstable, and names AI as the most plausible channel for another burst.
Ben Garfinkel looked at the same history and found very little support for the idea that growth follows one smooth speeding up curve.

chapters.caption: The chart shows only the shape of the two ideas, steady exponential growth and a curve that keeps steepening. It is not drawn from data.

chapters.lead: Forethought asks a sharp question: once AI can do all of AI research, could better algorithms alone, on the same chips, make progress speed up and up. It comes down to one number, r.
chapters.r_text: r is how many times AI software doubles each time the total research effort doubles. Above 1, each doubling comes faster than the last. Below 1, progress fizzles out. Exactly 1 is steady exponential growth.
chapters.bottom: Their best guess for AI software today is r of about 1 to 4. With chips held fixed they lower it to about 0.5 to 2. Software efficiency has been doubling about every 6 months.
chapters.src: Daniel Eth and Tom Davidson, Will AI R&D Automation Cause a Software Intelligence Explosion?, Forethought, 26 March 2025

chapters.lead: The biggest labs now say in writing that AI doing AI research is a danger sign. Here is what two of them committed to, in their own documents.

lines.t: AI self-improvement is a Tracked Category
lines.d: OpenAI split self-improvement out on its own because it can mean a hard to track, rapid speed up in AI capabilities. Its High level is reached when a model's impact is like giving every OpenAI researcher a highly capable mid-career research engineer assistant, compared with 2024. Reaching it requires High standard security controls.

lines.who: Anthropic Responsible Scaling Policy (update of 10 February 2026)
lines.t: AI R&D-4 needs an affirmative safety case
lines.d: Once a model crosses the AI R&D-4 capability threshold, Anthropic says it must write an affirmative case naming the most immediate misalignment risks from models pursuing misaligned goals, and explain how it has reduced them.

chapters.foot: These are company policies, not laws. Companies can change them, and outside groups argue about whether they are strong enough.

chapters.alt: A huge data center campus at dusk next to a power plant with steam rising
chapters.lead: An explosion still runs on electricity, factories and words. Epoch AI checked each limit and found room for a lot more scaling this decade.

limits.v: Data center campuses of 1 to 5 gigawatts are likely possible by 2030. Training spread across many sites could use 2 to 45 GW.
Planned chip output limits growth, along with packaging and high bandwidth memory.
About 300 trillion tokens of good public human text exist. At current trends models will use it all between 2026 and 2032.
The time it takes to pass data through a model sets a speed limit on how big a single training run can get.

big: training runs will likely be feasible by 2030
bigger than the models of 2024, about the jump from GPT-2 to GPT-4
chapters.src: Jaime Sevilla and others, Can AI Scaling Continue Through 2030?, Epoch AI, 20 August 2024. Pablo Villalobos and others, Will we run out of data?, Epoch AI, 6 June 2024.

chapters.alt: A dark control room with a wall of screens showing activity graphs and a few red alerts
chapters.h: Staying in control of a faster mind
chapters.lead: If AI starts doing most AI research, people need ways to stay safe even when they cannot fully trust the model. Two efforts show the hope and the difficulty.

duo.who: Ryan Greenblatt, Buck Shlegeris, Kshitij Sachan and Fabien Roger (Redwood Research), December 2023
duo.d: They build safety protocols that should hold even if the model is trying to get around them on purpose. One idea is to have a weaker model you trust watch a stronger model you do not, and send the most suspicious work to people.

OpenAI set out to solve how to align superintelligent systems within four years and promised 20% of its computing power. Employees later reported the compute never came, and the team's co-lead Jan Leike resigned in May 2024.

chapters.alt: A long hall whose walls are covered with thousands of signed letters
chapters.h: Tens of thousands signed their names
chapters.lead: Every few years a short statement asks the world to slow down or take the risk seriously. Signature counts are as shown on each page on 29 October 2026.

letters.ask: We call on all AI labs to immediately pause for at least 6 months the training of AI systems more powerful than GPT-4.
Mitigating the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority alongside other societal-scale risks such as pandemics and nuclear war.
We call for a prohibition on the development of superintelligence, not lifted before there is broad scientific consensus that it will be done safely and controllably, and strong public buy-in.

chapters.foot: The superintelligence count includes 5,000 signatures from a petition by Eko, as the page notes. See chapter 07 for the lab employees who signed Pacing the Frontier.

chapters.alt: A city at blue hour where delivery robots and driverless cars move along glowing lanes
chapters.h: Losing control without a single bang
chapters.lead: Not every bad ending looks like an explosion. A 2025 paper argues people could slowly lose their grip as AI takes over the work that keeps the economy, culture and states tied to human needs.

steps.v: As AI replaces human labour, firms and markets depend less on people, and what people want carries less weight.
More of what we read and watch is made by AI for AI driven systems, and human voices count for less.
Governments that need fewer citizens to work, fight or pay tax have weaker reasons to listen to them.
Each system weakens the others' ties to people, so the effects add up. The authors call this an existential risk that needs no rogue AI at all.

chapters.src: Jan Kulveit, Raymond Douglas, Nora Ammann, Deger Turan, David Krueger and David Duvenaud, Gradual Disempowerment, arXiv 2501.16946, January 2025
